title: The next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless: Built from the ground up for agents
key_points: OpenSearch Serverless re-architected with compute split from storage; new collections scale in seconds and down to zero when idle.
AWS reports up to 20x faster autoscaling and up to 60% lower cost than provisioning for peak; tutorial builds a vector collection.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Sohaib Katariwala, Arjun Nambiar, Raj Ramasubbu

title: How Zynga scaled multi-warehouse data governance with Amazon Redshift federated permissions
key_points: Zynga gave a game studio its own Redshift compute over the central warehouse's data and needed the same tiered access rules on every warehouse without a custom grant-sync job.
Redshift federated permissions plus IAM Identity Center let grants defined once apply across provisioned and Serverless consumers.
Practical detail: each read grant goes to both the Identity Center group and the federated IAM role used by service accounts, so people and pipelines see the same data.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon Redshift Serverless, AWS IAM Identity Center, AWS IAM
decision: Per-warehouse grants kept in sync by custom jobs vs federated permissions defined once across producer and consumer warehouses
authors: Zynga — Johan Eklund, Matthew Wongkee, Noelia Tardón, Sandeep Adwankar, Satesh Sonti, Steve Phillips

title: How Buildkite Operates Test Analytics at Massive Scale with Amazon MSK and Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
key_points: Buildkite's test analytics outgrew a Rails and PostgreSQL design, so ingestion moved to MSK with Managed Flink enriching and aggregating test results per tenant before they are served.
AWS reports 50 billion test executions a month and 500K events per second at peak, with webhook payloads up to 21 MB.
Story-level on fault tolerance and multi-tenancy; light on configuration detail.
services: Amazon MSK, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
decision: Database-centred ingestion vs streaming backbone (Kafka + Flink) for multi-tenant high-volume telemetry analytics
authors: Buildkite — James Hill, Masudur Rahaman Sayem, Miranda Li, Mitch James

title: Automate data discovery and centralized management with AWS Glue Data Catalog
key_points: When a new S3 bucket, RDS database or DynamoDB table appears, EventBridge and Lambda register it, a Glue crawler catalogues the schema and a PySpark Glue job scans it for PII.
Owner and purpose tags on the resource plus the PII results are written back into the Glue Data Catalog, with a DynamoDB table tracking each source's processing state.
Deployed as four CDK stacks from an AWS sample repo; turns a weeks-long manual inventory into an automatic one.
services: AWS Glue, AWS Glue Data Catalog, AWS Lambda, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon S3, AWS CDK
decision: Manual data inventory reviews vs event-driven cataloguing and PII scanning of every new data store
attaches_to: aws-bytes: governance (later); Data Quality Check (done) follow-up
authors: Ramakrishna Natarajan

title: How Amazon is moving to integrate catalogs to improve data discovery with Amazon SageMaker
key_points: Amazon's internal data team extended its enterprise catalog (Andes) with SageMaker so datasets, dashboards, metrics and local files are found in one place under one access model.
High-level story with little that transfers to a smaller platform.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon SageMaker Catalog
authors: Amazon — Pradeep Misra, Brad Porter (AWS), EunJi Kang, Gerry Moses, Matt David, Ramesh H Singh, Trevor Gasdaska

title: Automate deployment of data and AI applications with Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio CI/CD CLI
key_points: Open-source CLI for SageMaker Unified Studio: a data team describes a multi-service application (Glue jobs, Airflow DAGs, Quick dashboards, ML) once in a YAML manifest, and the CLI deploys it per stage with config substitution and ordering.
Walkthrough promotes a Glue ETL plus Quick dashboard app from dev to prod and wires it into GitHub Actions.
Bureau Veritas is the customer example for separating data-team and DevOps ownership.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, AWS Glue, Amazon MWAA, AWS Quick Sight, GitHub Actions
decision: Per-service IaC templates vs one manifest-driven deploy CLI for promoting data applications across stages
authors: Bureau Veritas — Saurabh Bhutyani, Amir Bar Or, Nikita Arbuzov, Ramesh H Singh, Vasudevan Venkataramanan

title: Meet Amazon Redshift RG – AWS Graviton-based instances with an integrated data lake query engine delivering up to 2.4x better performance at 30% lower price than RA3
key_points: Launch of RG, Graviton-based provisioned Redshift nodes with a new vectorized engine that also queries Iceberg and Parquet in the lake, and no separate Spectrum per-TB scan charge.
AWS reports up to 2.2x faster warehouse and up to 2.4x faster lake queries at 30% lower price per vCPU than RA3, with feature parity so clusters move without redesign.
Starts in two sizes (rg.xlarge, rg.4xlarge); RA3 and DC2 clusters modernize from the console.
services: Amazon Redshift, AWS Graviton, Amazon Redshift Spectrum, Apache Iceberg
decision: Stay on RA3/DC2 vs move to RG vs Redshift Serverless, now that lake scans carry no Spectrum charge on RG
authors: Ankit Sahu

title: Build petabyte-scale synthetic test data with Amazon EMR on EC2
key_points: Production data is off-limits for testing in regulated industries and TPC-DS lacks real business patterns, so the post generates realistic synthetic data with Spark and Faker on EMR.

Most of it is about making Faker scale: pooled Faker instances, fixed seeds for repeatable output, broadcast reference data, batched generation, and Spark settings such as Arrow, AQE and partition-aware writes.
Companion to the SQL engine benchmarking post, which uses this data.
services: Amazon EMR, Apache Spark, Amazon S3, Faker
decision: Masked production copies vs TPC-DS-style data vs custom synthetic generator for pipeline and performance testing
authors: Anubhav Awasthi, Gagan Brahmi, JP Boreddy, Sahil Thapar

title: A systematic approach to benchmarking SQL processing engines on AWS
key_points: Standard TPC-style benchmarks rarely predict how an engine behaves on a real workload, so the post lays out a repeatable way to compare Athena, Redshift, EMR and Trino on EKS with Apache JMeter over JDBC.

The method: pick representative query shapes, vary the data window, step up concurrency, weight how often each query runs at each step, and compare p90/p95 latency and throughput, sequential and concurrent.
Gives no results of its own; it is a test design, paired with a companion post on generating synthetic test data.
services: Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, Amazon EMR, Apache JMeter, Trino, Amazon EKS
decision: Athena vs Redshift vs Spark/Trino for a given workload, decided by a concurrency-weighted benchmark instead of TPC numbers
attaches_to: dbt-pipelines (Redshift Serverless vs Athena on NYC 311)
authors: Anubhav Awasthi, Gagan Brahmi, JP Boreddy, Sahil Thapar

title: OpenSearch Agent Skills bring built-in intelligence to your agentic IDE
key_points: Launch of an open repository of OpenSearch agent skills for AI coding tools, covering search relevance tuning, log analysis and Solr-to-OpenSearch migration.
Search-specific; nothing that touches the reader's pipelines.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Agent Skills
authors: Bobby Mohammed, Sean Zheng

title: How Smartsheet built Real-time Dynamic Filtering on Apache Flink reducing $40K/month in messaging costs
key_points: Smartsheet consumers subscribed to a huge SNS topic with static filter policies, so they pulled nearly every event and threw most away; filter changes also took minutes to apply.

They moved routing into Managed Flink: which sheets have active collaborators arrives as a change stream (DynamoDB Streams) and is held as broadcast state, and each event is matched against it in real time.
AWS reports over $40K per month saved on messaging and live-collaboration latency improved 1.8x.
services: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS, Amazon DynamoDB Streams
decision: Static broker-side subscription filters vs dynamic filtering in a stateful stream processor for high-volume event routing
authors: Smartsheet — Emre Kartoglu, Rony Blum, Francisco Morillo

title: Optimize Amazon S3 Tables queries with Amazon Redshift
key_points: Third part of the Redshift + S3 Tables series, aimed at repeated dashboard-style queries over Iceberg data that rescan S3 every time.

Three levers: external schemas through Lake Formation resource links to drop the three-part table names, Redshift materialized views that keep results local, and S3 Tables compaction tuned to the query pattern.
Compaction guidance: sort order for date-range filters, z-order when queries filter on several columns, plus snapshot housekeeping and MV refresh options.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, AWS Lake Formation, AWS Glue Data Catalog
decision: Query Iceberg in place vs Redshift materialized view vs re-laid-out files (binpack vs sort vs z-order compaction) for repeated lake queries
attaches_to: aws-bytes: File Layout Optimization (active); dbt-pipelines (Iceberg folder)
authors: Tom Romano, Satesh Sonti

title: Securing client confidentiality at scale: Automated data discovery and governed analytics for legal workloads
key_points: Reference architecture for law firms: documents stay in S3, Macie continuously classifies them, and analytics runs on Macie's findings rather than on copies of the documents.
The findings are catalogued with Glue and governed with Lake Formation tags mapped to client and matter, so ethical walls carry through to Quick dashboards and agents.
No build steps; the reusable idea is analysing discovery metadata instead of moving sensitive content.
services: Amazon Macie, Amazon S3, AWS Glue, AWS Lake Formation, AWS Quick, AWS Security Hub, Amazon SNS
decision: Copy sensitive documents into an analytics store vs analyse classification findings governed by tag-based access
authors: Rohan Kamat, Miguel Lopez Luis, Pranali Khose

title: Streamlined monitoring and debugging for Amazon EMR on EC2
key_points: From EMR 7.11, step, Spark driver and executor logs can stream to CloudWatch Logs natively, with no bootstrap actions or hand-configured agents.
Also adds per-step S3 logging controls, YARN and Tez UIs in the console, and a mapping from each EMR step to its YARN application ID for faster root-cause work.
Worth knowing what is now built in before building custom EMR log collection; the extra CloudWatch charges are noted.
services: Amazon EMR, Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon S3, Apache Spark
decision: Custom bootstrap log agents vs native CloudWatch Logs streaming vs S3-only logs for EMR job debugging
authors: Parul Saxena, Arun Prabakaran, Justin Mae, Ravi Kumar Singh, Lorenzo Ripani, Jason Zou

title: Detect and resolve HBase inconsistencies faster with AI on Amazon EMR
key_points: Collects HBase logs, HBCK consistency reports and metadata from EMR, embeds them into OpenSearch vector search, and lets operators ask an AI assistant (Kiro CLI) what is wrong.
AWS reports inconsistency resolution going from hours to minutes; the setup is specific to HBase operations.
services: Amazon EMR, Apache HBase, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Kiro
authors: Yu-Ting Su

title: Improve DynamoDB analytics with AWS Glue zero-ETL schema and partition controls
key_points: Glue zero-ETL replicates DynamoDB tables into Iceberg on S3 for Athena, and two setup choices decide how usable the result is: how far nested attributes get flattened and how the target is partitioned.
Compares no unnesting, one level, and full unnesting, and default vs identity vs time-based vs multi-level partitioning, with guidance on which suits which query pattern.
Ends by checking the flattened schema and partition pruning from Athena, which is the measurable part.
services: Amazon DynamoDB, AWS Glue, AWS Glue zero-ETL, Apache Iceberg, Amazon S3, Amazon Athena, Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse
decision: Keep nested vs partly vs fully flatten, and which partition scheme, when replicating DynamoDB to Iceberg with zero-ETL
attaches_to: aws-bytes: change data capture - DMS vs zero-ETL (later); File Layout Optimization (active)
authors: Raju Ansari, Shashank Sharma

title: How to use streamlined permissions for Amazon S3 Tables and Iceberg materialized views
key_points: S3 Tables registered in the Glue Data Catalog can now be governed with plain IAM policies covering storage, catalog and compute together; Lake Formation becomes an opt-in layer for fine-grained control.
Walkthrough creates an Iceberg materialized view from EMR Spark, then reads the same tables and view from Athena and Redshift under the IAM-only model.
A materialized view can live in S3 Tables or a general-purpose bucket regardless of where its base tables sit.
services: Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, AWS Glue Data Catalog, AWS IAM, AWS Lake Formation, Amazon EMR, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift
decision: IAM-only access vs Lake Formation fine-grained permissions for S3 Tables shared across engines
authors: Srividya Parthasarathy, Milind Oke, Pratik Das, Ricardo Serafim

title: How to build a cross-Region resilience for Amazon OpenSearch Service with Amazon MSK
key_points: Active-active OpenSearch across two Regions: writes go to MSK, MSK Replicator copies topics across Regions, and OpenSearch Ingestion in each Region feeds the local collection.
Avoids re-establishing replication on failback, unlike snapshot or cross-cluster replication approaches.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion, Amazon MSK, MSK Replicator
authors: Sriharsha Subramanya Begolli, Jay Jothi, Qais Poonawala

title: How to consolidate cross-Region S3 data into OpenSearch
key_points: OpenSearch Ingestion pipelines can now read S3 buckets in other Regions, both by scanning buckets and from SQS notifications for vended logs like VPC Flow Logs and CloudTrail.
Shows pipeline config for both modes to land everything in one OpenSearch domain or collection.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon S3, Amazon SQS
authors: David Venable

title: Enable real-time mainframe analytics with Precisely Connect and Amazon S3
key_points: Partner post: Precisely Connect now replicates mainframe change data directly into S3, without an intermediate Kafka hop.
S3 Tables, Athena, EMR and Redshift are presented as an optional analytics layer on top; the substance is the partner product.
services: Amazon S3, Amazon S3 Tables, AWS Mainframe Modernization, Precisely Connect
authors: Precisely — Supreet Padhi, Rochelle Grubbs, Tamara Astakhova

title: Migrating TLS Clients managed by third-party Certificate Authorities from self-managed Apache Kafka to Amazon MSK
key_points: Teams moving self-managed Kafka with mutual TLS to MSK normally have to reissue every client certificate from an AWS Private CA.
The post avoids that by creating an intermediate CA under the existing third-party root, importing it into AWS Private CA and pointing MSK at it, so old client certs keep working.
Mostly OpenSSL and certificate-chain steps plus handshake debugging.
services: Amazon MSK, AWS Private Certificate Authority, AWS Certificate Manager
authors: Ali Alemi, Swapna Bandla

title: Build streaming applications on Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink with AI-assisted guidance
key_points: An agent skill for Managed Service for Apache Flink plugs into AI coding tools (Kiro and others) and guides design, code review and connector choices from AWS best practices.
Demo builds a Kinesis-to-Kinesis Flink job from a conversation, then uses the skill to check an existing app for Flink 1.x to 2.2 incompatibilities and refactor it.
Useful mainly as a lower-friction way into Flink for someone who has not written a Flink app yet.
services: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Agent Toolkit for AWS, Kiro
decision: Hand-written Flink apps and manual version upgrades vs agent-guided build and 1.x-to-2.x migration
authors: Mazrim Mehrtens

title: A guide to capacity planning for Airflow worker pool in Amazon MWAA
key_points: Second part of the MWAA worker series: how to size workers before a known workload increase rather than after an SLA miss.
Method: read peak concurrent tasks from CloudWatch, project the growth, convert that into base and maximum workers with headroom, then set alarms that tell you when to revisit the plan.
Worked example is a financial-services team adding regulatory reporting DAGs, with a decision matrix for when to scale.
services: Amazon MWAA, Apache Airflow, Amazon CloudWatch
decision: Reactive scaling after SLA misses vs metric-based capacity planning before adding DAGs
authors: Boyko Radulov, Andrew McKenzie, Kamen Sharlandjiev, Harshawardhan Kulkarni, Venu Thangalapally

title: A guide to Airflow worker pool optimization in Amazon MWAA
key_points: Long task queues in MWAA tempt teams to add workers, but the cause is often elsewhere: heavy work running inside Airflow instead of on Glue/EMR, tight concurrency or pool settings, or slow memory leaks.
Walks through each symptom (high CPU, queue time, scheduling delay, idle workers) with the CloudWatch signals that tell a real capacity shortage apart from a misconfiguration.
Core message: fix the DAGs and settings first, scale workers only when the metrics still say so.
services: Amazon MWAA, Apache Airflow, Amazon CloudWatch
decision: Add workers vs tune Airflow concurrency/pool settings vs move heavy work out of the orchestrator for slow MWAA task queues
authors: Boyko Radulov, Andrew McKenzie, Kamen Sharlandjiev, Harshawardhan Kulkarni, Venu Thangalapally
